extracted.intended_audience: lawyers, judges, law students, and others researching evidentiary standards for expert testimony
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and factors used by U.S. courts to determine whether expert witness testimony is admissible under Rule 702 (the Daubert standard), including procedural timing for challenges and the scope of judicial gatekeeping.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judge is gatekeeper
rubrics_metrics.description: Under Rule 702 of the Federal Rules of Evidence, the task of 'gatekeeping', or assuring that scientific expert testimony truly proceeds from 'scientific knowledge', rests on the trial judge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The trial judge must perform gatekeeping to ensure expert testimony is scientific knowledge; this is a judicial responsibility rather than one left to the jury.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relevance and reliability
rubrics_metrics.description: The trial judge must ensure that the expert's testimony is 'relevant to the task at hand' and that it rests 'on a reliable foundation'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concerns about testimony cannot be simply left to the jury as a question of weight. The admissibility determination is governed by Rule 104(a), and the judge must find it more likely than not that the expert's methods are reliable and reliably applied to the facts at hand.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific knowledge = product of scientific methodology
rubrics_metrics.description: A conclusion will qualify as scientific knowledge if the proponent can demonstrate that it is the product of sound 'scientific methodology' derived from the scientific method.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Court described scientific methodology as formulating hypotheses and conducting experiments to prove or falsify them. Novel or contested science should be evaluated for reliability using these methodological criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Whether the theory or technique is generally accepted
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the theory or technique employed by the expert is generally accepted in the scientific community.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Listed by the Court as an illustrative factor; related to but not identical with the older Frye 'general acceptance' test. The Court cautioned that the Daubert list should not be treated as a mandatory checklist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Whether it has been subjected to peer review and publication
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the theory/technique has been subjected to peer review and publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Peer review and publication are illustrative indicators of reliability; the Court included this factor but warned factors are illustrative, not dispositive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Whether it can be and has been tested
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the technique or theory can be tested and whether it has been tested.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Testability (including experimental attempts to prove or falsify hypotheses) is an important indicium of scientific methodology; later phrasing on the page emphasizes testing in actual field conditions as well as laboratory tests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Whether it has a known error rate
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the technique has a known or potential rate of error.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identifying error rates and measures of uncertainty is an important factor in assessing reliability. The Court's illustrative factors specifically include known error rates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Whether standards exist for controlling the technique's operation
rubrics_metrics.description: Do standards exist for the control of the technique's operation?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Existence of standards/protocols for how to perform and control the technique supports reliability; the later list on the page explicitly includes this as a consideration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Whether the research was independent of the litigation
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the research was conducted independent of the particular litigation or dependent on an intention to provide the proposed testimony.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Research produced specifically for litigation (or in anticipation of providing testimony) may weigh against reliability; independence supports credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Has the technique been tested in actual field conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: Has the technique been tested in actual field conditions (and not just in a laboratory)?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Field validation as opposed to only laboratory validation is an explicit consideration on the page; helps assess external validity and applicability to the case facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Daubert factors are illustrative, not a definitive checklist
rubrics_metrics.description: The Supreme Court explicitly cautioned that the Daubert list should not be regarded by judges as 'a definitive checklist or test'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although courts often treat the factors as a checklist, the original opinion intended them to be flexible guideposts; judges should avoid rigid, mandatory application (Kumho noted that treating them as mandatory is erroneous).

rubrics_metrics.name: Daubert applies to all expert testimony (Kumho extension)
rubrics_metrics.description: The judge's gatekeeping function identified in Daubert applies to all expert testimony, including that which is non-scientific.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kumho Tire Co. v. Carmichael extended Daubert gatekeeping beyond strictly 'scientific' experts to technical and other specialized knowledge; courts must apply the same relevancy/reliability inquiry to non-scientific experts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appellate review standard: abuse of discretion
rubrics_metrics.description: A district court judge may exclude expert testimony when there are gaps between the evidence relied on by an expert and that person's conclusion, and an abuse-of-discretion standard of review is the proper standard for appellate courts reviewing such decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appellate courts defer to trial judges' gatekeeping decisions unless the exclusion represents an abuse of discretion; Joiner established this standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Admissibility governed by Rule 702 and preliminary questions under Rule 104(a)
rubrics_metrics.description: Admissibility of expert testimony is governed by Federal Rule of Evidence 702 and preliminary questions are resolved under Rule 104(a).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rule 702 sets the substantive criteria (testimony by qualified experts that will assist the trier of fact) while Rule 104(a) places the admissibility determination as a judge's preliminary question, requiring a finding by a preponderance of evidence as to reliability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing and procedural timing for Daubert motions
rubrics_metrics.description: A Daubert motion (often a motion in limine) may be brought prior to trial or during trial; it should be brought within a reasonable time after the close of discovery if the grounds can be anticipated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hearing should be scheduled well in advance of first trial calendar appearance. Courts have denied or admonished untimely motions filed too close to trial; in cases relying heavily on expert testimony, courts should set realistic discovery and trial schedules to allow parties to locate experts who meet Rule 702.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidentiary hearing may not always be necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: An evidentiary hearing on a Daubert motion may not be necessary if the court finds it would not assist in ruling on the motion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts may decide motions on papers or limited submissions; however, where expert testimony is central, a hearing is often advisable to develop the record and avoid reversible error.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical effects and potential for misuse
rubrics_metrics.description: Daubert can be used to exclude 'junk science' but has also been criticized for shifting burdens to plaintiffs and for potential attorney abuses (delay, cost-inflation) and for making judges act as amateur scientists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Awareness of practical consequences: exclusion can cause case dismissals; motions can be misused strategically; judges may lack scientific literacy, prompting calls for judicial education and institutional protocols for validation.
